title: Objects and responsibilities
objective: Give each class one clear job, so that one kind of change touches one place.

sources.title: Robert C. Martin, The Single Responsibility Principle (Clean Coder Blog, 2014)
David L. Parnas, On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules (Communications of the ACM 15(12), 1972)

simplifies: Classes show only the members that matter for the idea; real code adds error handling, transactions and tests. "One job" is a judgement call: split when parts change for different reasons, not into one class per method.

steps.caption: A shop's Order class does everything: it holds the items, adds up the total, saves itself to the database and emails the receipt.
The shop switches to a new email provider, so Order has to change: the same class that adds up prices. Any edit there risks breaking the totals.

predict.prompt: The shop switches to a new email provider. Which class has to change?

options.text: Order: the same class that adds up the prices
options.explanation: Right. Pricing, storage and email all live in Order, so every kind of change lands there.
There isn't one; sending email is inside Order.

options.text: None: email is outside the code
options.explanation: The code that sends the email is in email_receipt(), inside Order.

steps.caption: A useful test: how many different reasons does this class have to change? Pricing rules, the database, and email: three reasons, three jobs.
Split it by reason to change: Order keeps the items and the total; Store saves orders; Mailer sends receipts. Each class now has one job.
Order is now small and only about orders. Its code knows nothing about databases or email.
Something still has to run the steps in order. The shop's checkout asks Order for the total…
…asks the store to save the order…

predict.prompt: Next the receipt must go out. Who sends it?

options.text: The Mailer, asked by the shop
options.explanation: Right. Sending receipts is the Mailer's one job; the shop just coordinates.
That was the old design. Order no longer knows about email.
Saving and emailing are different jobs; joining them again would undo the split.

steps.caption: …and asks the Mailer to send the receipt. Changing email providers now means editing only the Mailer.

exercise.change: Receipts must also be sent by SMS.
exercise.hint: Look for the same job copied into more than one class.

options.text: Move sending messages into one Notifier class that Order, Refund and Invoice all use
options.explanation: Right. Sending becomes one job in one place, so a new channel is a one-class change.

options.text: Add send_sms() next to email_receipt() in each class
options.explanation: That works today, but it is three edits now and three more for every future channel.

options.text: Make Refund and Invoice inherit from Order to share email_receipt()
options.explanation: A refund isn't an order. Inheriting just to share code ties unrelated classes together (more on this in Composition versus inheritance).

exercise.explain: Sending messages is now one responsibility in one place. Order, Refund and Invoice change only when their own rules change, and the next channel (say, push notifications) is again a change to Notifier alone.

quiz.prompt: What does "one responsibility" mean for a class?

options.text: It has one reason to change: one set of rules it answers to
options.explanation: Right. Martin's wording: gather together the things that change for the same reasons.
A class can have many methods that all serve one job.

options.text: Only one other class uses it
options.explanation: How many classes use it says nothing about how many jobs it does.

quiz.prompt: A User class checks passwords, saves users to the database and draws the profile page. A designer changes the profile layout. What's the risk?

options.text: The layout edit happens inside User, next to the password and saving code, so it can break them
options.explanation: Right. Three jobs in one class means any change puts the other two at risk.

options.text: None: a layout change only touches HTML
options.explanation: The page is drawn inside User, so User itself has to change.
The layout doesn't affect what is stored.
